name: Raiju
description: Raiju (雷獣, 'thunder beast') is a legendary yōkai from Japanese mythology, the companion of Raijin the thunder god, whose body is composed of or wrapped in lightning. It descends during thunderstorms, becomes agitated, and may take many animal forms — most often a weasel, wolf, or cat — depending on the regional tradition.
full_description: Raiju (雷獣) is a legendary creature and yōkai in Japanese mythology, whose name translates as 'thunder beast' or 'thunder animal.' It is the companion of Raijin, the Shinto god of lightning, and its body is described as composed of or wrapped in lightning. During thunderstorms, the raiju descends from the heavens where it normally resides with Raijin, becoming agitated and leaping about in trees and buildings. Lightning-struck trees were said to bear claw marks left by the raiju. The creature's physical form is notably variable across time and region: most commonly it is depicted as a weasel-like creature, a white-blue wolf or dog with a split tail, a badger-like tanuki, a rabbit, a porcupine, a cat with bat-like flying membranes, or even a pure ball of lightning with no animal form. Western Japanese traditions describe dramatically different appearances, including crab or spider-like creatures with scaled pincer-tipped limbs. According to Edo-period belief, the raiju sleeps in human navels during calm weather — a belief that generated widespread anxiety, since Raijin, searching for his sleeping companion during storms, might strike the sleeping place with lightning, inadvertently killing the human host. This gave rise to protective customs against sleeping outdoors during storms. Several historical 'raiju relics' exist: Saishō-ji Temple in Niigata houses a mummy approximately 35 cm long identified by yōkai researcher Katsumi Tada as a domestic cat, and Yūzan-ji Temple in Iwate contains a mummy tagged 'Raijin.' Modern scholars identify the masked palm civet as the most likely basis for the raiju, given the animal's size, tree-climbing behavior, sharp claws, and tree-scratching habits. Many Edo-period raiju specimens displayed in sideshows were fabricated from weasels or badgers.

aliases.name: Raijuu
aliases.meaning: Alternative Hepburn romanization of the same term

origin: Raiju legends are primarily concentrated in East Japan, with notable regional variants throughout the Japanese archipelago. Most documented accounts come from the Edo period, with locations including Akita, Shinano, Echigo, Sagami, Aizu, Lake Biwa, and Akō.

etymology.origin: Japanese; compound of 雷 (rai, 'thunder/lightning') and 獣 (jū, 'beast/animal'). Legends are primarily concentrated in East Japan and were especially prominent during the Edo period (1603–1868).
etymology.first_use: Edo period (1603–1868) documentation; roots in older Shinto traditions associating animals with lightning phenomena

timeline.event: Earliest documented specific raiju account in extant sources (Akita region account)
timeline.source: Historical Japanese folklore sources from Edo period

timeline.event: Account describes a cat-like raiju with bat-like flying membranes
timeline.significance: One of the latest traditional raiju accounts before scientific explanations replaced folklore

timeline.event: Last documented traditional raiju account in extant sources (Akō region)
timeline.significance: End of the primary documentation period for raiju sightings

related.name: Raijin
related.description: The Shinto god of thunder and lightning; the raiju is his companion and servant

related.name: Nue
related.description: A yōkai defeated by Minamoto no Yorimasa in the Tale of the Heike; some scholars suggest the nue may have been a raiju

related.name: Thunderbird
related.description: North American Indigenous mythological creature associated with storms and lightning; functionally similar role

cultural_notes: During the Edo period the raiju was 'extremely well known' and reflected genuine anxiety about lightning. Protective practices (sleeping face-down, carrying specific protective items) were widespread.
